title: Clo Vendor Leaderboard: 3D Capacity
description:
We’re officially debuting the CLO Vendor Leaderboard, a platform created to connect brands with the most innovative 3D-ready partners in the industry. This year, we’re spotlighting pioneers across Hong Kong and Southeast Asia: Busana Apparel Group, Cobalt Fashion, Crystal International, GMS+, Hop Lun, Newtimes Group, Daehan Global, PT. Kahatex, and Trax Intertrade.

In the first CLO Vendor Leaderboard 5 criterias video series, we pull back the curtain on the 3D Capacity of the world’s most digitally advanced apparel partners. Discover how industry leaders are structuring their teams and optimizing their workflows using the CLO Ecosystem.

This series covers the 5 essentials of 3D success:
1️⃣ 3D Capacity 
2️⃣ Investment & Resources
3️⃣ Business Impact
4️⃣ Partnership
5️⃣ Strategic Vision

Timestamps:
0:00 - Introduction
0:13 - How is your 3D team structured, and what ongoing training or development programs do you offer to keep them at the forefront of CLO expertise?
03:35 - Can you walk us through a typical CLO workflow that produces high-quality virtual samples, highlighting the methods that make it faster or more accurate? How do you ensure consistency?
07:27 - What specific operational approaches (e.g., automation, 3D asset libraries, CLO-SET workflows, SOPs) have you introduced to expand 3D capacity, and what measurable effect have they had?

👇 Comment below: What’s your biggest challenge in scaling 3D production?
transcript: Our 3D team operates globally. This structure allow us to collaborate seamlessly across time zones, ensuring continuous workflow and rapid project turnaround for a single client or collection. We rely on the strong 3D foundations that our 3D designers and technicians bring with them and supplement with our in-house virtual quality standard. This internal guidelines ensure that 3D garments are interpreted consistently. Our 3D team is built around super flexible designers who can do it all, creating patterns, working with digital fabrics and designing trims, or using clothes. This setup lets everyone jump in whenever needed, making us quick and adaptable. We run hands-on workshops, especially on AI tools that keep us ahead of the curve. We have a centralized 3D design and development team that is skilled and trained to work across multiple product categories and to support new developments and client presentations. Alongside that, we have product-specific teams that focus on brand and category-specific 3D work. Both the central team and the product teams regularly participate in CLO training. And we complement that with internal knowledge sharing, so that they stay at the forefront of CLO and 3D practices. The 3D teams are divided between tech and design, each working independently. Our in-house training program covers all the latest CLO features in different levels, with relevant 3D news and technology demos. We also have an internal training program for data consumption, and a 3D standard training for brands. In addition, we update software functions by checking the latest version in time, ensuring that we maintain up-to-date technology and competitiveness. We have a specialized 3D team that focuses on the aspect of digital product creation in CLO. Our team consists of a combination of specialists who have long experience in 3D digital product creation, and new talent. so that we can combine in-depth expertise with innovative new perspectives. To ensure that our team continues to develop CLO expertise, we undergo continuous training and development. With a combination of external training and continuous internal learning, our 3D team has been able to be flexible and ready to adapt to challenges or changes in the industry of apparel and textiles. Our 3D team is structured by strength rather than hierarchy. One member specializes in fabric digitization and physics, and the other handles garment construction. The other focuses on rendering and presentation. By keeping everyone in their area of expertise, they speed up the delivery and maintain consistency. For our team skill development, we run monthly CLO skill shares and do quick demos whenever someone discovers a new workflow. All this allocates time for us. We also offer external training for CLO masterclasses. The mindset is simple – learn fast, share immediately, and keep the team moving forward. We ensure consistency through clear internal SOPs, standardized presets, and approved asset libraries. All of this is managed with disciplined version naming. On top of that, we have peer reviews at critical checkpoints. For example, fit, drape, color, or graphic, which helps us maintain a uniform quality level across all teams and styles. So our CLO workflow is designed to produce high-quality, efficient, and consistent digital samples. One of the main aspects of our process is to use the automated 3D quality check function from Closet. After the sample is made, our special 3D checker or QA specialist does a comprehensive review, supported by the automation done by Closet. This tool helps us to quickly identify problems such as fitting, pattern construction, and visual accuracy, so that we can handle it proactively. This significantly reduces revision and repetition time. This collaborative approach, which is combined with automatic quality assurance, ensures that each digital sample we produce has high accuracy and consistency. To ensure consistency across all projects, we rely on a centralized internal material library that is continuously updating the new yarn scans, color panels, and gauge data. This guarantees that every 3D and knitting artist is working with standardized, verified assets, resulting in result and technological accurate digital samples across global teams. Our 3D workflow is straightforward but packed with small steps to make it fast and accurate. With importing or quickly modifying a block pattern in Closet, then assign real scan fabrics, simulate add trims, and then render high-res turntable or stills. What makes it fast, accurate, and consistent is that we have extensive brand-specific templates for blocks, fits, and fabrics, so most garments start 70-80% done. And everything that we work with lives in a shared library with brand standards, and internal measurements are checked, so everyone is starting from the exact same approved assets. We create dedicated algorithms and blocks or silhouettes for each brand we work with. Our dedicated 3D technicians do all the fabric digitalization, knee pattern, and stitching, but send them to our designer for the look development and output. To ensure the brand identity and look is presented correctly, make sure the same technician and designer are used for specific brands, so they are familiar with the individual requirements for each. Our 3D workflow is built around consistency and speed. What makes this process fast is that around 40% of 3D styles we don't build from scratch. We utilize reusable templates, calibrate fabric presets, and clear naming conventions. This ensures every style looks like it came from the same team, no matter who worked on it. And what turns speed into accuracy is we leverage our internal SOPs and quality standards. Which allow us to confidently deliver high-quality 3D prototypes. Our team uses standardized methods to create a core brand database, database, and hardware. This strategy allows us to maintain consistency throughout the development process, ensuring that each virtual sample meets the brand characteristics and quality standards. By utilizing these standardized assets, we simplified the workflow, reduced the variability, and increased efficiency. To expand our 3D capacity, one of the main operational ways we apply is to integrate 3D prototype creation from the beginning in the development process, especially as part of the visibility check. By using Claw, to create digital samples in the early stages, we can more easily check whether this design is suitable or the construction challenge before making physical samples. This way provides many benefits that can be measured. The number of inaccurate physical samples or does not need to be greatly reduced, and the development time is automatically shorter. With the 3D prototype at the beginning of the process, our team's capacity is increasing, but the quality and consistency are still maintained. In addition, we have a wide range of innovative digital assets libraries, including silhouettes, alphabets, fabrics, and trims. All these assets, along with the styles we develop, are centralized and stored on the ClawSets platform. For a new customer, we rapidly customize designs and develop different configurations and executions by swapping out elements like fabrics, colors, prints, trims, and labeling. This has made presenting live reviews and customer intros demos much easier and faster. We have built three assets and applied the ClawSets workflow to quickly integrate resources, save time, and enhance the ability to quickly process and render repeatable designs.
markdown_content: ## Global CLO 3D Team Structure and Operating Model This section describes how the global CLO 3D team is organized to maintain continuous workflow across time zones, with centralized standards and both central and product-specific support. The 3D team operates globally to collaborate seamlessly across time zones, enabling continuous workflow and rapid project turnaround for a single client or a collection. The team relies on strong 3D foundations from its designers and technicians, supplemented by an in-house virtual quality standard. Internal guidelines ensure 3D garments are interpreted consistently. The team is designed around highly flexible designers who can handle multiple tasks, including creating patterns, working with digital fabrics, and designing trims (as well as related garment work). This allows team members to jump in whenever needed, improving speed and adaptability. A centralized 3D design and development team supports multiple product categories and new developments, including client presentations. Alongside this, product-specific teams focus on brand- and category-specific 3D work. Both the central team and product teams regularly participate in CLO training, supported by internal knowledge sharing to stay current with CLO and 3D practices. ## Team Skill Development, Training, and Continuous Learning This section covers the internal and external training programs, including CLO feature training, data consumption training, brand-specific standards, and ongoing technical updates. The 3D teams are divided between tech and design, each working independently. Training is structured to cover CLO capabilities at different levels, including the latest CLO features and relevant 3D news and technology demos. There is also internal training for data consumption and a dedicated 3D standard training for brands. The team continuously maintains tool readiness by checking the latest software versions in time to keep technology up to date and competitive. To build long-term CLO expertise, the team uses both external training and continuous internal learning, enabling flexibility and readiness for changes in apparel and textiles. ## CLO Workflow Organization: Strength-Based Roles and Checkpoints This section explains how the team is split by technical strengths (fabric physics, garment construction, rendering) and how peer reviews and checkpoints support consistent quality. The team is structured by strength rather than hierarchy. Roles are specialized as follows: - One member focuses on fabric digitization and physics. - Another handles garment construction. - Another focuses on rendering and presentation. Specialization within each area helps speed delivery while maintaining consistency. For skill development, the team runs monthly CLO skill shares and performs quick demos whenever someone discovers a new workflow. External training is also offered through CLO masterclasses. Quality consistency is enforced via clear internal SOPs, standardized presets, and approved asset libraries. Version naming is managed in a disciplined way. Peer reviews occur at critical checkpoints—such as fit, drape, color, and graphic—helping maintain a uniform quality level across teams and styles. ## Automated 3D Quality Assurance Using Closet This section details the use of Closet’s automated 3D quality check and how QA specialists validate fit, pattern construction, and visual accuracy to reduce revisions. A core part of the process is using the automated 3D quality check function from Closet. After a sample is created, a specialized 3D checker/QA specialist performs a comprehensive review supported by Closet automation. The tool helps quickly identify problems including: - Fitting issues - Pattern construction issues - Visual accuracy issues By handling problems proactively, the team significantly reduces revision and repetition time. Combined with automatic quality assurance, this approach ensures each digital sample has high accuracy and consistency. ## Standardized Assets and Centralized Material Libraries This section explains how the team maintains consistency using a centralized internal material library with continuously updated yarn scans, color panels, and gauge data. To ensure consistency across projects, the team uses a centralized internal material library that is continuously updated with new yarn scans, color panels, and gauge data. This guarantees that every 3D and knitting artist works from standardized, verified assets, producing digitally accurate and technologically correct samples across global teams. All work relies on shared libraries containing brand standards and internal measurements. This ensures everyone starts from the exact same approved assets, reducing variability across teams. ## Fast, Consistent CLO 3D Production Steps This section outlines the practical workflow steps in Closet: pattern import/modification, scan fabric assignment, trim simulation, and rendering outputs. The 3D workflow is described as straightforward but broken into small steps to keep production fast and accurate. A typical flow includes: 1. Importing or quickly modifying a block pattern in Closet 2. Assigning real scan fabrics 3. Simulating added trims 4. Rendering high-resolution turntable or still images Speed, accuracy, and consistency are supported by extensive brand-specific templates for blocks, fits, and fabrics. Most garments are started at approximately 70–80% completion using these templates. Everything is managed in shared brand-standard libraries, with internal measurements checked so work begins from approved assets. Dedicated algorithms and blocks (silhouettes) are created for each brand. Dedicated 3D technicians handle fabric digitalization, knee pattern, and stitching, then send outputs to designers for look development and final output. ## Brand-Specific Consistency: Templates, Naming, and Same-Team Ownership This section covers how the workflow preserves brand identity using reusable templates, calibrated fabric presets, clear naming conventions, and consistent pairing of technicians and designers per brand. To present brand identity and look correctly, the same technician and designer are used for specific brands so they understand individual brand requirements. The workflow is built around consistency and speed, supported by reusable templates, calibrated fabric presets, and clear naming conventions. The process targets efficiency by not building all 3D styles from scratch. Approximately 40% of 3D styles are created using reusable resources rather than full rebuilds. Standardized methods support a core brand database (and related data structures) and the overall development approach, ensuring each virtual sample meets brand characteristics and quality standards. By using standardized assets, the team reduces variability and increases efficiency while delivering high-quality 3D prototypes. ## Expanding CLO 3D Capacity Early in Development (Visibility Checks) This section explains integrating 3D prototype creation from the beginning—especially for visibility checks—to reduce inaccurate physical samples and shorten development time. To expand 3D capacity, the team integrates 3D prototype creation from the beginning of the development process, particularly as part of visibility checks. Using Claw to create digital samples early helps the team assess whether: - the design is suitable, and - the construction challenges are acceptable before producing physical samples. This early approach provides measurable benefits: it reduces the number of inaccurate physical samples that don’t need to be greatly repeated, and it shortens development time. With 3D prototypes early, capacity increases while maintaining quality and consistency. ## Centralized Digital Asset Libraries and ClawSets Workflow This section describes how the team manages reusable digital assets (silhouettes, alphabets, fabrics, trims) and uses the ClawSets platform to rapidly customize and deliver repeatable configurations. The team maintains a wide range of innovative digital asset libraries, including silhouettes, alphabets, fabrics, and trims. These assets, along with developed styles, are centralized and stored on the ClawSets platform. For new customers, the team rapidly customizes designs by swapping elements such as: - fabrics - colors - prints - trims - labeling This enables faster live reviews and customer intro demos. The team applies the ClawSets workflow to quickly integrate resources, save time, and improve the ability to process and render repeatable designs.
